lines: This is VerifiQuant, governance by execution for financial LLM workflows.
It is joint work by Yu-Chi Ko, Mi-Yen Yeh and Shou-De Lin, at National Taiwan University and Academia Sinica.
The one-line version is: keep the spreadsheet, and let the LLM fill it in.
LLMs in finance now sit in workflows that end in a number.
Valuation memos, client calculators, regulatory reports.
They rarely fail by crashing.
They fail with a clean, wrong number, and nothing marks it as wrong.
Program-aided reasoning fixes the arithmetic, because an interpreter runs the code.
But it does not decide whether the question justifies a number at all.
Here is a real trap from our evaluation.
It asks for a stock’s price rate of change over one week.
We changed the opening price from 150 dollars to 2.5 dollars.
R-PAL sees the same retrieved contracts and runs code. It reports 6,500 percent.
R-PAL plus also gets every one of our checks described in its prompt.
It still reports 6,500 percent, in all three runs.
VerifiQuant stops at gate E in all three runs, and shows the check that failed: a weekly price change above 200 percent.
Same model, same contracts. The difference is whether the check is executed or only described.
So the question we ask is not how accurate the system is.
It is when a number may leave the system at all.
Every response is one of three things: a correct number, a silent wrong, or a named exit that says why.
The goal is to turn silent wrongs into named exits, while keeping as many correct numbers as possible.
There are five reasons a question may not justify a number, and each gets a letter.
N: nothing in the library covers the question.
M: the intent is unclear, like “the return” without saying holding-period or annualized.
F: a required input is missing.
E: a value breaks a declared check, like that 2.5-dollar price.
I: a convention is left open, like whether payments come at the start or the end of each period.
These letters are also the gates of the pipeline.
To catch them, we borrow from how analysts already work.
An analyst does not re-derive a loan formula for each client.
They open a vetted sheet, type in the inputs, and the sheet refuses impossible values.
We write each formula family once as such a sheet. We call it a Financial Inference Contract.
The library holds 250 of them, generated offline and checked with lint and smoke tests. None was hand-tuned.
The LLM gets three jobs, and only three.
Pick the sheet. Fill the input cells. Flag which declared conventions the text leaves open.
It never computes the answer, and it never freely rewrites the formula.
This is the real loan contract, drawn as a sheet.
The orange rows are what the LLM fills: principal, rate and term.
The blue rows are data validation, run as code. The principal must be positive, and the rate must stay below 1.0.
Then come declared conventions.
Rate scale is hard, because it changes the computation, so the system asks.
Payment timing is soft, because it changes how you read the number, so the system answers and warns.
The green row is locked Python code, which returns 1,498.88.
Now suppose the LLM binds “6 percent” as 6 instead of 0.06.
The rate check fails, and the query ends at an alert that names the check. No number leaves.
At run time, every query goes through this funnel, from left to right.
Retrieval is BM25 over the contracts, top four.
Then three LLM steps, in orange, alternate with code steps, in blue.
Select picks one contract, or none. Bind fills the inputs.
Code then checks that every required input is present, and that every declared boundary holds.
The ambiguity step asks whether a convention is still open.
Only a query that passes every gate reaches the contract’s own code.
Every stop is a named exit.
N refuses. M asks which quantity you meant. F asks for the missing field by name.
E names the failed check and the bound value.
For conventions, a soft one returns the number with a warning.
A hard one asks the user to pick a declared option, and then applies a verified edit.
Every path, with a number or without one, writes a DiagnosticReport that replays from the stored binding.
Now the main result.
We derived 80 traps from the contracts: 20 each of missing input, impossible value, open convention, and out of scope.
We count how often a system still gives an unqualified number. We call this false numeric acceptance.
R-PAL plus has our whole checklist in its prompt, and it still answers 27.5 percent of the traps.
VerifiQuant runs the same checks in stages, and answers 10.4 percent.
That is 17 points lower, with a 95 percent interval from about 7 to 27 points.
Every system uses Gemini 2.5 Flash and the same top-four contracts, averaged over three runs.
Where does the gap come from? Boundary and ambiguity traps.
On impossible values, R-PAL plus accepts 30 percent, and VerifiQuant 8.3.
On open conventions, 80 percent against 21.7.
There, the right answer depends on an executed check or an unstated convention.
On missing inputs and out-of-scope questions, a prompt already refuses, and VerifiQuant is no better.
Plain R-PAL, which only runs code, answers 48.8 percent of all traps.
This is not an accuracy result.
On 250 well-posed questions, R-PAL reaches 96.8 percent accuracy.
VerifiQuant reaches 81.2 percent, because it declines about 16 percent of them.
Its silent-wrong rate stays close to R-PAL’s, 2.8 against 2.4 percent.
The grey row is an upper bound, not a deployment result.
There, an oracle that knows the intended computation, but never the answer, may clarify up to twice. Accuracy then reaches 93.6 percent.
This chart puts safety and utility on one picture.
Coverage on clean questions runs across. False acceptance on traps runs up. The ideal is the lower right.
The two hollow points test whether the gain comes only from splitting the prompt into stages.
Staging alone reaches 15.8 percent, but only by refusing much more.
Staging plus the contract text ties VerifiQuant on traps, at 8.8 percent, but covers only 75 percent of clean questions.
So staging over the declared contract lowers false acceptance, and running the contract’s own code keeps coverage.
Measured against R-PAL plus, each trap number avoided costs VerifiQuant 2.0 correct clean answers.
One more technical piece: what happens when a user picks a non-default convention.
The computation has to change. If the LLM rewrote the code, it would reopen the door the funnel just closed.
So every edit is declared on the contract at build time.
For the loan, paying at the start of each period means dividing by one plus the monthly rate.
The invariant says: multiply back, and you recover the old payment.
The payment moves from 1,498.88 to 1,491.42.
Before the edit runs, three checks.
Bounded: 13 syntax-tree nodes, the declared limit.
Safe: whitelisted names only.
Matches: the invariant holds on five sampled inputs.
To test the verifier, we generated 906 faulty patches on purpose.
27 turned out to be equivalent to the original.
Of the other 879, the verifier rejects 97.7 percent, including every structural attack.
20 get through.
This is bounded numerical validation, not a formal proof.
Most of the 20 sit in branches that none of the sampled inputs reached.
Outside the library, we ran two separate tests.
First, we rebuilt the library from 50 formula families, so 199 questions have no matching contract.
VerifiQuant abstains on 88.9 percent of them.
R-PAL abstains on half a percent. It is right 95 percent of the time from memory, but gives no signal when it is wrong.
So out of library, VerifiQuant is not more accurate. What it offers is a scope signal.
Second, five finance-trained annotators labeled 80 natural queries blind.
On the 46 that call for no number, the ordering holds, but only the gap to plain R-PAL is significant.
To be clear about the boundary.
The claim holds for single-number, formula-grounded questions inside the library, with a correct contract.
The silent wrongs that remain trace to three LLM steps: selection, binding, and recalling a convention.
The gates check schema and bounds, not where a value came from.
And this is not a compliance claim. Traceable records are a design target.
So: keep the spreadsheet, and let the LLM fill it in.
It pays wherever an unflagged wrong number costs more than a declined question, as in valuation, reporting, and client-facing calculation.
If coverage is all you need, R-PAL is the better choice.
The live demo at verifiquant.com replays every trap from the paper.
The QR codes on screen link to the demo, the code, and the paper. Thank you.
